title: At COP31, Bangladesh asks for three times more adaptation finance
excerpt: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman met President Erdogan in Antalya on 10 November and delivers Bangladesh's statement to the plenary on 12 November.
content:
Bangladesh is asking countries at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to triple international finance for adaptation and to give it as grants rather than loans, Bangladesh Post and bdnews24.com reported. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, who leads the delegation, met Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on the sidelines on Tuesday evening, 10 November.

What Bangladesh is asking for

  • A threefold increase in international adaptation finance.
  • Grant-based finance for adaptation and loss and damage, so it does not add to national debt, with simpler approval processes.
  • A larger, working Loss and Damage Fund, with easier access through funds such as the Green Climate Fund, especially for coastal areas.
  • Technology transfer for agriculture and water security, support for the National Adaptation Plan, early warning systems and mangrove and wetland conservation.
  • Holding warming to 1.5°C, with faster emissions cuts by developed countries.

Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo said “grants, rather than loans, should be increased” for adaptation and loss and damage, Bangladesh Post reported. He told bdnews24.com that climate change costs Bangladesh about $15.2 billion a year. Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury said Bangladesh produces only 0.05% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

The Erdoğan meeting

The two leaders discussed trade, defence industry cooperation, the Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar and climate risks such as floods, A News reported. Erdoğan said Türkiye would keep the Rohingya situation in the international spotlight and suggested its “Climate Implementation Bridge” initiative could help Bangladesh with flood management and resilient infrastructure. Prothom Alo reported that the prime minister’s visit runs from 10 to 12 November and that he will deliver Bangladesh’s national statement at the plenary on 12 November.

Why it matters

Whether more adaptation money arrives, and in what form, decides how much support reaches flood, cyclone and salinity-hit communities where many NGOs work. A Change Initiative study this month found that 92% of energy-sector climate finance to Bangladesh came as loans, which is why the government is pressing on grants. Tripling is a negotiating ask; no figure has been agreed.

What to watch

  • The prime minister’s plenary statement on 12 November and any new pledges from donors.
  • Whether the final COP31 decision, due by 20 November, sets a new adaptation finance goal.
